reason: The early prose Upaniṣads name the goal 'immortality'; the later ŚU and MaiU use mokṣa for release from saṃsāra; the equivalence is interpretive and the early texts do not themselves equate the words.
ChU 8.1.1 locates the small space (dahara) within the lotus of the heart; the two are related, not identical.
The mahāvākyas state the identity; recorded as a standpoint-relative sameness because the later schools dispute its sense.
BAU 3.7 and MāU 6 describe the inner controller with lordly functions.
The later lists of vital currents include the five Upaniṣadic breaths.
Later readers relate the ChU's three colours and ŚU 4.5's red-white-black ajā to the three guṇas; the ChU does not name guṇas.

change: bands: rungs 1-15 B2; bhūman B5; ātmādeśa/svarāj B7
reason: The rungs are venerations (preparatory meditative discipline); bhūman is the first seeing of plenitude; the self-ruled knower shown the far shore corresponds to final liberation.
Restraint of speech and mind is withdrawal; merging into the great self is absorption with support; the peaceful self is the goal.
The first instruction is the entry point beyond which the qualified student must pass; the last is the goal.

change: bands: bliss B5, knower's song B8
reason: Bliss as brahman is the culminating recognition; the song describes the knower's free activity afterwards.
Renunciation is the entry; learning is preparatory study; the muni's silence deepening; the brahmin the knower.
BS 2.1.17 reads asat as the unmanifest by the continuation of the passage; partially reconciled; candidate readings kept.
The persons are limited objects of veneration; brahman is the self — the text's own ranking.
Ritual learning kept but placed below knowledge of the self within all.
Six partial views as parts of one whole, by the text itself.
The body-self as the first stage of a graded teaching; the text's rejection of it as a final view is recorded.

change: equivalents prc:omkara-dhyana and prc:pranava-japa graded partial
reason: Meditation on Om in the Upaniṣads (upāsanā, abhidhyāna) overlaps with Purāṇic Om-meditation and Yoga's Om-repetition but is not described as repetition.
Both internalize the agnihotra into the breaths; KauU offers speech and breath into each other, ChU offers food into the five breaths.
Five of the Maitrī's six limbs share names with Patañjali's limbs; tarka and the order differ.
